screens.title: Creating Your First ROS Package and Node
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn the concrete steps to create a ROS package, add dependencies, and write simple nodes in both Python and C++. We begin by using the catkin_create_pkg command to scaffold a package and then examine the two files that control build and runtime behavior: package. xml and CMakeLists. txt. You will see how a Python script becomes an executable node after a chmod, and how a C++ program must be declared in CMakeLists and compiled with catkin_make. We'll also practice running nodes with rosrun and using anonymous node names so multiple instances can coexist. Each step matters because the package is the unit ROS uses to distribute code, messages, and launch definitions. A typical hands-on activity will have you create my_first_robot, write a small Python node that prints a countdown, write the equivalent C++ node, build, and run both. As you go, watch for common misconceptions: package. xml controls metadata and dependency declarations, while CMakeLists controls compilation; missing a dependency in package. xml will break build or runtime. By the end you'll be able to scaffold, implement, build, and launch simple nodes and inspect running nodes with rosnode list.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Creating Your First ROS Package and Node
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Create, build, and run your first ROS package

You will scaffold a package, inspect manifest and build files, write both Python and C++ nodes, and run them using catkin tools. This gives you the minimum full cycle for ROS development.

Package Preview
my_first_robot · depends: std_msgs, geometry_msgs, roscpp, rospy
In this lesson

Scaffold a package with catkin_create_pkg, inspect package.xml and CMakeLists, write a simple Python node and a C++ node, build with catkin_make, and run with rosrun. Practice anonymous node names and using rosnode list.

Coming up
  • Package scaffold and structure
  • Python and C++ node examples
  • Build and run workflow
Why this matters

Packages make ROS projects reusable, discoverable, and buildable. Knowing this cycle means you can iterate quickly and integrate with other ROS components.

Quick Commands
cd ~/catkin_ws/src
catkin_create_pkg my_first_robot std_msgs geometry_msgs roscpp rospy
Explore Key Topics
Scaffold
Use catkin_create_pkg to create a package with dependencies declared in package.xml.
Nodes
Write small executable programs in scripts/ or src/ and initialize with the ROS client API.
Build & Run
Use catkin_make and source setup to compile and run C++ nodes and rosrun to launch nodes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to create a catkin package with the correct dependencies, inspect and edit package. xml and CMakeLists. txt, write simple nodes in both Python and C++, and run them using the standard catkin and rosrun tools. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: scaffolding packages so file layout is correct, understanding the roles of manifest and build files so dependencies are handled properly, writing nodes that register with the ROS master so they communicate correctly, and building and executing C++ nodes with catkin_make. For example, after creating my_first_robot you will add a Python script into scripts/, make it executable, and verify it appears with rosnode list after running. These are foundational developer competencies: without them you cannot reliably share code, create custom messages, or integrate multiple nodes. Practice each objective in sequence: scaffold, inspect metadata, implement nodes, build, and run. That sequence prevents common errors like forgetting to declare a dependency or failing to make Python scripts executable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — continued
screens.narratorSegment: This continuation focuses on two more practical skills: writing C++ nodes that initialize and use NodeHandle, and managing node names and anonymous instances. Writing a C++ node requires declaring executables in CMakeLists and linking against catkin libraries so compilation produces a runnable binary. You will practice adding an add_executable and target_link_libraries directive and then building with catkin_make. The other objective is about node identity: ROS requires unique node names; using anonymous names in Python appends an identifier so you can run multiple copies without one being deregistered. You'll see why that matters when running duplicate sensor processes or test nodes. Concrete practice includes editing CMakeLists to add my_first_cpp_node, compiling, sourcing setup, and launching both the Python and C++ nodes. Finally, you will verify with rosnode list and observe unique names for anonymous instances. These are small, repeatable steps that prevent common errors during development and integration.

screens.title: What is a ROS package?
screens.narratorSegment: A ROS package is the fundamental unit for organizing software in ROS. It bundles source code, message and service definitions, launch configurations, and metadata that other tools use to build and run your code. Think of a package as a small project folder with a strict contract: package. xml declares what the package needs, and CMakeLists. txt instructs the build system how to compile and install components. For example, when you run catkin_create_pkg my_first_robot std_msgs geometry_msgs roscpp rospy, you create a folder with a package manifest and a CMake template so other developers and the build tools can find dependencies and build rules. A common misconception is that package. xml alone controls building; in reality, package. xml informs dependency resolution, while CMakeLists controls the compilation steps, especially for C++ code and message generation. Practically, packages live in the src directory of your workspace so catkin_make can discover them. Use a clear layout—scripts for Python, src for C++—so both interpreted and compiled nodes are easy to find. A good question to keep in mind: does this package include anything others will need, like custom messages or launch files? If yes, include msg, srv, or launch directories so they are part of the package contract.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › What is a ROS package?
Definition

A package contains source code, message definitions, launch files, and metadata so ROS tools and other developers can build and use your functionality.

Structure example
my_first_robot/
├── package.xml
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── src/
├── scripts/
├── msg/
└── launch/
Concrete benefit
Other developers can discover dependencies and build your components; tools can generate message headers and compile binaries.
Key Takeaway

Treat packages as portable project units. Declare everything needed in package.xml and keep code organized by language in scripts/ and src/.

Analogy & common misconception
Analogy: a package is like a small library with its own README, dependencies, and build instructions so it can be used by bigger projects.
Misconception: package.xml is not the full build script—CMakeLists controls compilation for C++ and message generation rules.
Question to reflect: does this package expose messages or services others will need? If so, include msg/ and srv/ directories.
Try this
Create a new folder in src/ named my_first_robot and add an empty package.xml and CMakeLists to see how catkin tools react.

screens.title: Scaffolding a package with catkin_create_pkg
screens.narratorSegment: Scaffolding a package is the first hands-on step. Use the catkin_create_pkg command in the src directory of your workspace and list the runtime and build dependencies you expect to use. For example, running catkin_create_pkg my_first_robot std_msgs geometry_msgs roscpp rospy creates a directory with package. xml and CMakeLists. txt and placeholders for src, scripts, and other standard folders. The dependencies you list are written into package. xml so rosdep and other tools can resolve them. A common error is running the command outside the src folder or forgetting a required dependency; if the dependency is missing at build time, catkin_make will fail or message headers will not be generated. After scaffolding, open package. xml to confirm and entries and note which dependencies you need at compile time versus runtime. Practice: scaffold my_first_robot, then open the generated files to see the default entries. Ask yourself which packages must be present for C++ compilation and which are only needed at runtime for Python scripts. Scaffolding a package with catkin_create_pkg means run catkin_create_pkg in src and list dependencies to generate the manifest and build template the right way.. In practical terms, command, typical dependencies, and what gets created. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Scaffolding a package with catkin_create_pkg
Terminal demo (example command)
cd ~/catkin_ws/src
catkin_create_pkg my_first_robot std_msgs geometry_msgs roscpp rospy
What is created: package.xml, CMakeLists.txt and placeholders for src/, scripts/, msg/, srv/.
Why list deps: they populate package.xml so rosdep and the build system know what to install and link.
Common mistake: running outside src/ or omitting a dependency you later need for compilation.
Inspecting the manifest
<package format="2">
  <name>my_first_robot</name>
  <build_depend>roscpp</build_depend>
  <build_depend>rospy</build_depend>
  <exec_depend>rospy</exec_depend>
</package>
Example check
Confirm that packages used only at runtime are under exec_depend and compile-time needs like roscpp appear under build_depend.
Pro tip

If you plan C++ code, include roscpp as a build_depend. If only Python nodes, python-related libs belong in exec_depend.

screens.title: Understanding package.xml
screens.narratorSegment: The package. xml file is the manifest that declares metadata and dependencies for a ROS package. It includes the package name, version, description, maintainer, license, and lists of dependencies separated by purpose. Build dependencies are packages needed at compile-time, such as C++ client libraries or message generators. Exec dependencies are required at runtime, such as Python client libraries or runtime message packages. An important practical point: some packages appear in both lists when they are needed during build and at run time — std_msgs often behaves this way because its headers are generated and used during compilation and its message types are required at runtime. A common misconception is that moving a dependency between tags is purely cosmetic; in practice, omitting a build dependency will break the compile stage, and omitting an exec dependency can cause a node to fail at runtime. Example: add build_depend roscpp for C++ nodes, and exec_depend rospy if your Python node uses rospy. Always run rosdep to install missing dependencies after editing package. xml. Reflect: when you add a new message type or library, which dependency tag should you update?

keyIdea.text: package.xml lists metadata and dependencies; use build_depend for compile-time needs and exec_depend for runtime needs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Understanding package.xml
Core elements
  • Name, version, description: basic metadata for the package.
  • Maintainer and license: who owns it and legal terms.
  • build_depend: packages needed to compile this package.
  • exec_depend: packages needed when the package runs.
Example snippet
<build_depend>roscpp</build_depend>
<exec_depend>rospy</exec_depend>
Practice and checks
Run rosdep after editing package.xml to install missing system dependencies.
Remember: if your package defines custom messages, you must list message generation dependencies and ensure they are present at build time.
Question: if a header is missing during C++ compile, which dependency tag likely needs updating? The answer is build_depend.
Common mistake

Forgetting to add message-generation dependencies will cause missing headers during C++ builds; check CMakeLists and package.xml together.

screens.title: Role of CMakeLists.txt
screens.narratorSegment: CMakeLists. txt is the build script that tells catkin how to compile and link C++ sources, generate message headers, and install executables. When you add a C++ node you must declare an add_executable target with the source path and then link it to ${catkin_LIBRARIES}. For example, adding add_executable(my_first_cpp_node src/my_first_node. cpp) and target_link_libraries(my_first_cpp_node ${catkin_LIBRARIES}) instructs the build system to produce a binary called my_first_cpp_node. The CMake file also controls message generation steps if you define custom messages or services. A frequent mistake is to forget to list include_directories with ${catkin_INCLUDE_DIRS} or to forget to call catkin_package, which can cause link-time or include-path issues. For pure Python packages, CMakeLists can be minimal, but for any C++ code it's required. Practically, after updating CMakeLists run catkin_make in the workspace root and then source devel/setup. bash before running the new binary. Think of CMakeLists as the map that converts source files into runnable artifacts. Role of CMakeLists.txt means cmakelists converts sources into binaries and triggers message generation; declare executables and link libraries here for c++ nodes.. In practical terms, how cmakelists controls c++ builds, executables, and message generation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Build Instructions
keyIdea.text: CMakeLists converts sources into binaries and triggers message generation; declare executables and link libraries here for C++ nodes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Role of CMakeLists.txt
CMake example (key lines)
add_executable(my_first_cpp_node src/my_first_node.cpp)
target_link_libraries(my_first_cpp_node ${catkin_LIBRARIES})
include_directories(${catkin_INCLUDE_DIRS})
Ensure catkin_package() is present so downstream packages can find your headers and libraries.
For message generation add the appropriate find_package and add_message_files rules before catkin_package.
Build workflow
  1. cd ~/catkin_ws
  2. catkin_make
  3. source devel/setup.bash
  4. rosrun my_first_robot my_first_cpp_node
Pro tip

If you change CMakeLists or add new source files, always rebuild with catkin_make and re-source the setup file before running binaries.

screens.title: Package directory structure
screens.narratorSegment: A predictable package layout makes development and collaboration much easier. The canonical structure includes package. xml and CMakeLists at the root, src/ for C++ source files, scripts/ for Python executable scripts, include/ for C++ headers, msg/ and srv/ for custom messages and services, and launch/ for XML launch files that start multiple nodes. Place interpreted Python nodes in scripts/ and mark them executable with chmod so rosrun can execute them directly. C++ sources belong in src/ and must be declared in CMakeLists to produce binaries. If you add custom message types, put their. msg files in msg/ and update both CMakeLists and package. xml so message generation occurs during catkin_make. A common confusion is putting Python files in src/ — while Python may run from anywhere, scripts/ is the conventional location and eases packaging and installation. Example: put scripts/my_first_node dot P Y file with a shebang and executable permissions, and src/my_first_node. cpp for the compiled counterpart. This organization ensures build tools and other developers find your artifacts without guessing. Package directory structure means keep interpreted scripts in scripts/, compiled sources in src/, and message definitions in msg/ to align with ros tooling.. In practical terms, where to put python scripts, c++ sources, messages, and launch files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Package directory structure
Directory map
my_first_robot/
├── package.xml
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── src/        # C++ sources
├── scripts/    # Python executables
├── include/    # C++ headers
├── msg/        # message types
└── launch/     # launch files
Practical notes
  • scripts/ should contain executable Python nodes with a proper shebang and chmod.
  • src/ and include/ support C++ source and header organization so CMake can find them.
  • msg/ and srv/ are required if you define custom message or service types; update both files accordingly.
Key Takeaway

Use the conventional folders so build and run tools behave as expected and collaborators can find code quickly.

screens.title: Writing a simple Python node
screens.narratorSegment: Writing a Python node is often the fastest way to get started. The Python client library provides a simple global A P I: you initialize the runtime by calling a library function to register the node name with the ROS master, and then you can use logging and sleep utilities for simple behaviors. A minimal node prints a message, sleeps for two seconds, and shuts down. Save the script in scripts/ and make it executable with chmod so rosrun can run it. The anonymous name option appends a unique suffix so you can run multiple copies simultaneously without name collisions; this is useful for testing or when you have multiple identical sensors. A common pitfall is forgetting the executable bit or the shebang line at the top, which prevents rosrun from executing the script directly. Example script saved as scripts/my_first_node dot P Y file prints a greeting, sleeps, and logs shutdown messages. After making it executable, run it with rosrun my_first_robot my_first_node dot P Y file and then inspect running nodes with rosnode list to confirm it registered with the master.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Writing a simple Python node
Code example
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy

if __name__ == '__main__':
    rospy.init_node('my_first_python_node', anonymous=True)
    rospy.loginfo("Hello, ROS! This is my first Python node.")
    rospy.sleep(2.0)
    rospy.loginfo("Node is shutting down.")
Make it executable: chmod +x scripts/my_first_node.py
Run: rosrun my_first_robot my_first_node.py
Explanation and checks
  • init_node registers the node with the ROS master so it can communicate.
  • anonymous=True appends a unique suffix so multiple instances do not conflict.
  • rospy.loginfo writes to the ROS logging system instead of standard print for integrated logs.
Common mistake

Forgetting the shebang or the executable bit prevents rosrun from launching the script; verify with ls -l.

#include <ros/ros.h>

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    ros::init(argc, argv, "my_first_cpp_node");

screens.title: Building with catkin_make and sourcing
screens.narratorSegment: Building with catkin_make compiles C++ targets, generates message headers, and prepares the workspace for runtime. screens.title: Running nodes with rosrun and verifying with rosnode list
screens.narratorSegment: Once your nodes are in place and the workspace is sourced, you can execute them with rosrun. The rosrun command requires the package name and the executable or script name. For example, rosrun my_first_robot my_first_node dot P Y file runs a Python script in scripts/, and rosrun my_first_robot my_first_cpp_node runs a compiled C++ binary. After launching, use rosnode list to query the ROS master for active nodes. This lets you confirm that nodes registered correctly and see their exact names. A key behavior to note is node name uniqueness: if two nodes attempt to register with the same name, the second will cause the first to be deregistered unless the second uses an anonymous suffix. To observe this, run two Python instances with anonymous names and then run rosnode list to see unique entries. Common confusion comes from rosrun not finding a node; usually this indicates either the package is not sourced into the environment or the executable name differs from the declared target. Verify with ls and by checking CMakeLists or the scripts folder. Closing question: after running and listing nodes, can you identify which nodes are anonymous instances and why?

If two nodes use identical names, the second will replace the first on the master. Use anonymous naming in Python to avoid this when running duplicates.

screens.title: Custom messages, services, and where to put them
screens.narratorSegment: If your package needs custom message or service types, include them in the msg/ and srv/ directories and update both CMakeLists and package. xml so the build system generates language-specific code. Place. msg files into msg/ and. srv files into srv/ and then add add_message_files and add_service_files blocks in CMakeLists along with generate_messages and appropriate dependencies. The package must list message-generation dependencies in package. xml so headers and types are available during build. A common misconception is that custom messages are only needed at runtime; in fact, message generation happens during build, so missing declarations will cause compile errors. For beginner tasks in this chapter, you may not need custom messages, but knowing where to place them and how to enable generation prepares you for extending nodes to carry structured data. Reflect: when would you add a custom message instead of reusing std_msgs? If your data structure is specific to your robot and shared across multiple nodes, a custom message is appropriate. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn the concrete steps to create a ROS package, add dependencies, and write simple nodes in both Python and C++. We begin by using the catkin_create_pkg command to scaffold a package and then examine the two files that control build and runtime behavior: package. xml and CMakeLists. txt. You will see how a Python script becomes an executable node after a chmod, and how a C++ program must be declared in CMakeLists and compiled with catkin_make. We'll also practice running nodes with rosrun and using anonymous node names so multiple instances can coexist. Each step matters because the package is the unit ROS uses to distribute code, messages, and launch definitions. A typical hands-on activity will have you create my_first_robot, write a small Python node that prints a countdown, write the equivalent C++ node, build, and run both. As you go, watch for common misconceptions: package. xml controls metadata and dependency declarations, while CMakeLists controls compilation; missing a dependency in package. xml will break build or runtime. By the end you'll be able to scaffold, implement, build, and launch simple nodes and inspect running nodes with rosnode list.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to create a catkin package with the correct dependencies, inspect and edit package. xml and CMakeLists. txt, write simple nodes in both Python and C++, and run them using the standard catkin and rosrun tools. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: scaffolding packages so file layout is correct, understanding the roles of manifest and build files so dependencies are handled properly, writing nodes that register with the ROS master so they communicate correctly, and building and executing C++ nodes with catkin_make. For example, after creating my_first_robot you will add a Python script into scripts/, make it executable, and verify it appears with rosnode list after running. These are foundational developer competencies: without them you cannot reliably share code, create custom messages, or integrate multiple nodes. Practice each objective in sequence: scaffold, inspect metadata, implement nodes, build, and run. That sequence prevents common errors like forgetting to declare a dependency or failing to make Python scripts executable.

This continuation focuses on two more practical skills: writing C++ nodes that initialize and use NodeHandle, and managing node names and anonymous instances. Writing a C++ node requires declaring executables in CMakeLists and linking against catkin libraries so compilation produces a runnable binary. You will practice adding an add_executable and target_link_libraries directive and then building with catkin_make. The other objective is about node identity: ROS requires unique node names; using anonymous names in Python appends an identifier so you can run multiple copies without one being deregistered. You'll see why that matters when running duplicate sensor processes or test nodes. Concrete practice includes editing CMakeLists to add my_first_cpp_node, compiling, sourcing setup, and launching both the Python and C++ nodes. Finally, you will verify with rosnode list and observe unique names for anonymous instances. These are small, repeatable steps that prevent common errors during development and integration.

A ROS package is the fundamental unit for organizing software in ROS. It bundles source code, message and service definitions, launch configurations, and metadata that other tools use to build and run your code. Think of a package as a small project folder with a strict contract: package. xml declares what the package needs, and CMakeLists. txt instructs the build system how to compile and install components. For example, when you run catkin_create_pkg my_first_robot std_msgs geometry_msgs roscpp rospy, you create a folder with a package manifest and a CMake template so other developers and the build tools can find dependencies and build rules. A common misconception is that package. xml alone controls building; in reality, package. xml informs dependency resolution, while CMakeLists controls the compilation steps, especially for C++ code and message generation. Practically, packages live in the src directory of your workspace so catkin_make can discover them. Use a clear layout—scripts for Python, src for C++—so both interpreted and compiled nodes are easy to find. A good question to keep in mind: does this package include anything others will need, like custom messages or launch files? If yes, include msg, srv, or launch directories so they are part of the package contract.

Scaffolding a package is the first hands-on step. Use the catkin_create_pkg command in the src directory of your workspace and list the runtime and build dependencies you expect to use. For example, running catkin_create_pkg my_first_robot std_msgs geometry_msgs roscpp rospy creates a directory with package. xml and CMakeLists. txt and placeholders for src, scripts, and other standard folders. The dependencies you list are written into package. xml so rosdep and other tools can resolve them. A common error is running the command outside the src folder or forgetting a required dependency; if the dependency is missing at build time, catkin_make will fail or message headers will not be generated. After scaffolding, open package. xml to confirm and entries and note which dependencies you need at compile time versus runtime. Practice: scaffold my_first_robot, then open the generated files to see the default entries. Ask yourself which packages must be present for C++ compilation and which are only needed at runtime for Python scripts. Scaffolding a package with catkin_create_pkg means run catkin_create_pkg in src and list dependencies to generate the manifest and build template the right way.. In practical terms, command, typical dependencies, and what gets created. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The package. xml file is the manifest that declares metadata and dependencies for a ROS package. It includes the package name, version, description, maintainer, license, and lists of dependencies separated by purpose. Build dependencies are packages needed at compile-time, such as C++ client libraries or message generators. Exec dependencies are required at runtime, such as Python client libraries or runtime message packages. An important practical point: some packages appear in both lists when they are needed during build and at run time — std_msgs often behaves this way because its headers are generated and used during compilation and its message types are required at runtime. A common misconception is that moving a dependency between tags is purely cosmetic; in practice, omitting a build dependency will break the compile stage, and omitting an exec dependency can cause a node to fail at runtime. Example: add build_depend roscpp for C++ nodes, and exec_depend rospy if your Python node uses rospy. Always run rosdep to install missing dependencies after editing package. xml. Reflect: when you add a new message type or library, which dependency tag should you update?

CMakeLists. txt is the build script that tells catkin how to compile and link C++ sources, generate message headers, and install executables. When you add a C++ node you must declare an add_executable target with the source path and then link it to ${catkin_LIBRARIES}. For example, adding add_executable(my_first_cpp_node src/my_first_node. cpp) and target_link_libraries(my_first_cpp_node ${catkin_LIBRARIES}) instructs the build system to produce a binary called my_first_cpp_node. The CMake file also controls message generation steps if you define custom messages or services. A frequent mistake is to forget to list include_directories with ${catkin_INCLUDE_DIRS} or to forget to call catkin_package, which can cause link-time or include-path issues. For pure Python packages, CMakeLists can be minimal, but for any C++ code it's required. Practically, after updating CMakeLists run catkin_make in the workspace root and then source devel/setup. bash before running the new binary. Think of CMakeLists as the map that converts source files into runnable artifacts. Role of CMakeLists.txt means cmakelists converts sources into binaries and triggers message generation; declare executables and link libraries here for c++ nodes.. A predictable package layout makes development and collaboration much easier. The canonical structure includes package. xml and CMakeLists at the root, src/ for C++ source files, scripts/ for Python executable scripts, include/ for C++ headers, msg/ and srv/ for custom messages and services, and launch/ for XML launch files that start multiple nodes. Place interpreted Python nodes in scripts/ and mark them executable with chmod so rosrun can execute them directly. C++ sources belong in src/ and must be declared in CMakeLists to produce binaries. If you add custom message types, put their. msg files in msg/ and update both CMakeLists and package. xml so message generation occurs during catkin_make. A common confusion is putting Python files in src/ — while Python may run from anywhere, scripts/ is the conventional location and eases packaging and installation. Example: put scripts/my_first_node dot P Y file with a shebang and executable permissions, and src/my_first_node. cpp for the compiled counterpart. This organization ensures build tools and other developers find your artifacts without guessing. Package directory structure means keep interpreted scripts in scripts/, compiled sources in src/, and message definitions in msg/ to align with ros tooling.. In practical terms, where to put python scripts, c++ sources, messages, and launch files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Writing a Python node is often the fastest way to get started. The Python client library provides a simple global A P I: you initialize the runtime by calling a library function to register the node name with the ROS master, and then you can use logging and sleep utilities for simple behaviors. A minimal node prints a message, sleeps for two seconds, and shuts down. Save the script in scripts/ and make it executable with chmod so rosrun can run it. The anonymous name option appends a unique suffix so you can run multiple copies simultaneously without name collisions; this is useful for testing or when you have multiple identical sensors. A common pitfall is forgetting the executable bit or the shebang line at the top, which prevents rosrun from executing the script directly. Example script saved as scripts/my_first_node dot P Y file prints a greeting, sleeps, and logs shutdown messages. After making it executable, run it with rosrun my_first_robot my_first_node dot P Y file and then inspect running nodes with rosnode list to confirm it registered with the master.

A C++ node follows a similar logical structure to a Python node but requires compilation. The program calls a client-library function to initialize the runtime with a node name and then constructs a NodeHandle which is the main interface for creating publishers, subscribers, services, and reading parameters. A minimal C++ node prints a message using the ROS logging macro and sleeps using a ROS duration. Save the source in src/my_first_node. cpp and then add an add_executable and a target_link_libraries line to CMakeLists so catkin_make compiles it into a binary. After building and sourcing the workspace, you run the binary with rosrun my_first_robot my_first_cpp_node. A common misconception is thinking C++ behaves like interpreted Python; C++ must be rebuilt after changes. Example source demonstrates init, NodeHandle construction, ROS_INFO logging, and a duration sleep before clean exit. This pattern is the basis for creating more complex publishers and subscribers using the NodeHandle interface. Writing a simple C++ node means c++ nodes must be compiled and linked; initialize the node and use nodehandle to create communication primitives.. Building with catkin_make compiles C++ targets, generates message headers, and prepares the workspace for runtime. The standard flow is to run catkin_make from the workspace root, then source devel/setup. bash to configure your shell environment so rosrun and roslaunch can find newly built packages and executables. If you recently changed CMakeLists or added new source files, run catkin_make again; failing to re-run it is a frequent cause of missing binaries. After a successful build, verify that the binary exists under devel or install paths and then source the setup file. Sourcing ensures that ROS_PACKAGE_PATH and other environment variables reference the workspace. For example, cd ~/catkin_ws; catkin_make; source devel/setup. bash prepares you to run rosrun my_first_robot my_first_cpp_node or rosrun my_first_robot my_first_node dot P Y file. If rosrun cannot find a node, check that you sourced the correct setup file and that the executable name matches the target declared in CMakeLists or the filename in scripts. This sequence is the standard compile-and-run loop for ROS development. Once your nodes are in place and the workspace is sourced, you can execute them with rosrun. The rosrun command requires the package name and the executable or script name. For example, rosrun my_first_robot my_first_node dot P Y file runs a Python script in scripts/, and rosrun my_first_robot my_first_cpp_node runs a compiled C++ binary. After launching, use rosnode list to query the ROS master for active nodes. This lets you confirm that nodes registered correctly and see their exact names. A key behavior to note is node name uniqueness: if two nodes attempt to register with the same name, the second will cause the first to be deregistered unless the second uses an anonymous suffix. To observe this, run two Python instances with anonymous names and then run rosnode list to see unique entries. Common confusion comes from rosrun not finding a node; usually this indicates either the package is not sourced into the environment or the executable name differs from the declared target. Verify with ls and by checking CMakeLists or the scripts folder. Closing question: after running and listing nodes, can you identify which nodes are anonymous instances and why?

If your package needs custom message or service types, include them in the msg/ and srv/ directories and update both CMakeLists and package. xml so the build system generates language-specific code. Place. msg files into msg/ and. srv files into srv/ and then add add_message_files and add_service_files blocks in CMakeLists along with generate_messages and appropriate dependencies. The package must list message-generation dependencies in package. xml so headers and types are available during build. A common misconception is that custom messages are only needed at runtime; in fact, message generation happens during build, so missing declarations will cause compile errors. For beginner tasks in this chapter, you may not need custom messages, but knowing where to place them and how to enable generation prepares you for extending nodes to carry structured data. These are the core concepts to retain: first, a ROS package is the unit of distribution containing code, manifests, and message definitions. Second, use catkin_create_pkg to scaffold a package and declare dependencies in package. xml so the build system and rosdep can resolve them. Third, CMakeLists. txt contains build instructions for C++ code and message generation; update it when adding C++ sources or custom messages. Fourth, Python nodes are executable scripts placed in scripts/ and require chmod, while C++ nodes live in src/ and must be compiled. Fifth, build with catkin_make and always source the workspace setup file before running nodes. Finally, use rosrun to execute nodes and rosnode list to verify running node names; use anonymous names in Python to run multiple instances. Keep this checklist near your terminal until these steps become muscle memory.

Keep three short reminders in mind. First: Always declare dependencies — package. xml tells tools what your package needs. Second: Know the folder roles — scripts/ for Python, src/ and include/ for C++, msg/ and srv/ for custom types. Third: Build and source — catkin_make then source setup makes new code visible for rosrun. These short rules will help you avoid the most common early mistakes and let you iterate quickly when creating nodes, building packages, and integrating components.
